'''''Camellia japonica''''', known as '''common camellia''',<ref>{{Cite book|url=http://www.forest.go.kr/kna/special/download/English_Names_for_Korean_Native_Plants.pdf|title=English Names for Korean Native Plants|publisher=[[Korea National Arboretum]]|year=2015|isbn=978-89-97450-98-5|location=Pocheon|page=385|access-date=4 January 2017|via=[[Korea Forest Service]]|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170525105020/http://www.forest.go.kr/kna/special/download/English_Names_for_Korean_Native_Plants.pdf|archive-date=25 May 2017}}</ref> or '''Japanese camellia''', is a [[species]] of [[flowering plant]] from the genus ''[[Camellia]]'' in the [[tea]] family [[Theaceae]]. It is native to [[China]] and [[Japan]],<ref name="MAP C.japonica,rusticana"/> and grows naturally in [[forest]]s at altitudes of around {{convert|300|–|1100|m|ft|sigfig=2}}.<ref name=MinBartholomew/>

There are thousands of [[cultivar]]s of ''C. japonica'', with many colors and forms of [[flower]]s, mainly as [[garden]] [[ornamental plant]]s. The [[floriculture]] of ''Camellia japonica'' started in China. Its widespread cultivation can be traced back to the [[Song Dynasty]], when 15 varieties of ''Camellia japonica'' were recorded in literature.<ref name="Botanica 176"/>

==Description==
[[File:Kamelie Knospe.JPG|thumb|A bud of a Japanese camellia]]
''Camellia japonica'' is a flowering [[tree]] or [[shrub]], usually {{convert|1.5|–|6|m|ft}} tall, but occasionally up to {{convert|11|m|ft}} tall. Some cultivated varieties achieve a size of 72 m<sup>2</sup> or more. The youngest branches are purplish brown, becoming grayish brown as they age.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Japanese Camellia – Camellia japonica – The University of Alabama Arboretum |url=https://arboretum.ua.edu/whats-growing-on/japanese-camellia-camellia-japonica/ |access-date=2025-03-14 |website=arboretum.ua.edu}}</ref>

=== Leaves ===
The alternately arranged leathery leaves are dark green on the top side, paler on the underside, usually {{convert|5|–|11|cm|in}} long by {{convert|2.5|–|6|cm|in|1}} wide with a stalk ([[petiole (botany)|petiole]]) about {{convert|5|–|10|mm|in|1}} long. The base of the leaf is pointed (cuneate), the margins are very finely toothed (serrulate) and the tip somewhat pointed.<ref name="MinBartholomew" /> The leaves are rich in [[anti-inflammatory]] [[terpenoid]]s such as [[lupeol]] and [[squalene]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Majumder |first1=Soumya |last2=Ghosh |first2=Arindam |last3=Bhattacharya |first3=Malay |date=August 2020 |title=Natural anti-inflammatory terpenoids in Camellia japonica leaf and probable biosynthesis pathways of the metabolome |journal=Bulletin of the National Research Centre |volume=44 |issue=1 |page=141 |doi=10.1186/s42269-020-00397-7 |issn=2522-8307 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

=== Flower ===
In the wild, flowering is between January and March. The flowers appear along the branches, particularly towards the ends, and have very short stems. They occur either alone or in pairs, and are {{convert|6|–|10|cm|in}} across.{{citation needed|date=March 2023}}

There are about nine greenish [[bract]]eoles and [[sepal]]s. Flowers of the wild species have six or seven rose or white [[petal]]s, each {{convert|3|–|4.5|cm|in}} long by {{convert|1.5|–|2.5|cm|in|1}} wide; the innermost petals are joined at the base for up to a third of their length. (Cultivated forms often have more petals.) The numerous [[stamen]]s are {{convert|2.5|–|3.5|cm|in|1}} long, the outer whorl being joined at the base for up to {{convert|2.5|cm|in|1}}. The three-lobed [[style (botany)|style]] is about {{convert|3|cm|in}} long.<ref name=MinBartholomew/>

The Japanese white eye bird (''[[Zosterops japonicus]]'') pollinates ''Camellia japonica''.<ref name="Roubik et al"/> ''C. japonica'' flowers are important resources for flower-feeding insects and are visited by a number of insects, most of which are not pollinators but consumers. ''Dasiops'' sp. ([[Diptera]]) exploit flower buds. ''[[Drosophila]] unipectinata'', ''D. oshimai'', and ''D. lutescens'' (Diptera) and ''[[Epuraea]] commutata'' ([[Coleoptera]]) exploit fully opened, late, and fallen flowers.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Mitsui |first1=Hideyuki |last2=Kimura |first2=Masahito T. |date=2019 |title=Distribution pattern and competition of insects breeding on Camellia japonica flower |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/ens.12343 |journal=Entomological Science |language=en |volume=22 |issue=1 |pages=98–104 |doi=10.1111/ens.12343 |issn=1343-8786|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

=== Fruit ===
The [[fruit]] consists of a globe-shaped capsule with three compartments ([[locule]]s), each with one or two large brown [[seed]]s with a diameter of {{convert|1|–|2|cm|in|1}}. Fruiting occurs in September to October in the wild.<ref name=MinBartholomew/>

==Taxonomy==
The genus ''Camellia'' was named after a Jesuit priest and botanist named [[Georg Joseph Kamel|Georg Kamel]].<ref name="Cothran" /> The specific epithet ''japonica'' was given to the species by Carl Linnaeus in 1753. Despite its common name, ''Camellia japonica'' is indigenous to China. Camellia japonica has been growing wild since prehistoric times in the [[Kantō region]] of western Japan, southern Korea, Taiwan,  Zhejiang and Jiangsu.<ref name="MAP C.japonica,rusticana"/> In the Song Dynasty, 15 varieties of it were recorded in literature. The reason ''Camellia japonica'' got its name was that Engelbert Kaempfer was one of the first Europeans to give a description of the plant when he first saw it in Japan.

Two varieties are distinguished in the ''[[Flora of China]]'': ''C. japonica'' var. ''japonica'' and ''C. japonica'' var. ''rusticana''<ref name=MinBartholomew/><ref name="Flora of China"/>

===''Camellia japonica'' var. ''japonica''===

''C. japonica'' var. ''japonica'' is the form named by Linnaeus, and naturally occurs in forests at altitudes of {{convert|300|–|1100|m|ft}} in Shandong, eastern Zhejiang in mainland China and in Taiwan, south Japan, and South Korea.<ref name="MAP C.japonica,rusticana"/> The leaf has a [[Glossary of botanical terms#glabrous|glabrous]] stem ([[petiole (botany)|petiole]]) about {{convert|1|cm|in|1}} long. The bracteoles and sepals are velutinous (velvety). It flowers between January and March, and fruits in between September and October.<ref name="Flora of China"/> It is grown as a garden plant in the form of many cultivars throughout the world.

===''Camellia japonica'' var. ''rusticana''===
[[File:Camellia japonica var. decumbens 3.JPG|thumb|260px|right|''C. japonica'' var. ''rusticana'' in the wild, Aizu area, Fukushima pref., Japan]]
''Camellia japonica'' var. ''rusticana'' naturally occurs in forests in China.<ref>''Camellia japonica'' var. ''rusticana'' (Honda) T.L.Ming in GBIF Secretariat (2023). GBIF Backbone Taxonomy. Checklist dataset <nowiki>https://doi.org/10.15468/39omeiaccessed</nowiki> via GBIF.org on 2026-01-07.</ref> The leaf has a shorter petiole, about {{convert|5|mm|in|1}} long, with fine hairs (pubescent) at the base. The bracteoles and sepals are smooth (glabrous) on the outside. The color of the flowers ranges from red through rose to pink, flowering in April to May. This variety is regarded by some botanical authorities to be a separate species: ''Camellia rusticana''.<ref name="C. rusticana"/>

In Japan it is known by the common name "yuki-tsubaki" (snow camellia) as it naturally occurs in areas of heavy snowfall at altitudes ranging from {{convert|3500|ft|m|order=flip}} down to {{convert|400|ft|m|order=flip}} on sloping land under deciduous beech trees in the mountain regions to the north of the main island of Honshu and facing the [[Sea of Japan]].<ref name="MAP C.japonica,rusticana"/> In December heavy drifts of snow come in from the north, covering the plants to a depth of up to {{convert|8|ft|m|order=flip}}. The bushes remain covered by snow from December till the end of March when the snow melts in early Spring and the camellias start flowering.<ref name="E. G. Waterhouse"/>

Cultivars of ''C. japonica'' var. ''rusticana'' include: 'Nishiki-kirin', 'Nishiki-no-mine', 'Toyo-no-hikari' and 'Otome'.{{citation needed|date=March 2023}}

==History==

===China===
[[File:Japanese Camellia bonsai 55, December 24, 2008.jpg|thumb|A [[bonsai]] specimen of ''C. japonica'']]
''Camellia japonica'' has appeared in paintings and porcelain in China since the 11th century. Early paintings of the plant are usually of the single red flowering type. However, a single white flowering plant is shown in the scroll of the ''Four Magpies'' of the [[Song Dynasty]].<ref name="Valder">Valder, Peter. The Garden Plants of China. Oregon: Timber Press, 1999. {{ISBN|0-88192-470-9}}</ref>

===Australia===
[[File:02 Camelia.jpg|thumb|''Camellia japonica'' 'Aspasia Macarthur']]
The first records of camellias in Australia pertain to a consignment to [[Alexander Macleay]] of Sydney that arrived in 1826 and were planted in Sydney at [[Elizabeth Bay House]].<ref name="history-of-camellias-in-australia"/>

In 1838 six ''C. japonica'' plants were imported by the botanist, horticulturist and agriculturist [[William Macarthur]]. During the years that followed he brought in several hundred varieties and grew them at [[Camden Park Estate]].<ref name="CamelliasInAustralia"/> For many years Macarthur's nursery was one of the main sources of supply to the colony in Australia of ornamental plants, as well as fruit trees and vines.<ref name="history-of-camellias-in-australia"/>

In 1845, William Macarthur wrote to the London nurseryman [[Loddiges|Conrad Loddiges]], acknowledging receipt of camellias and mentioning: "I have raised four or five hundred seedlings of camellia, chiefly from seeds produced by 'Anemoniflora'. As this variety never has anthers of its own, I fertilised its blossoms with pollen of ''C. reticulata'' and Sp. ''maliflora''." Although most of Macarthur's seedling varieties have been lost to cultivation, some are still popular today, including 'Aspasia Macarthur' (named after him).<ref name="history-of-camellias-in-australia"/>

A well-known camellia nursery in Sydney was "Camellia Grove", set up in 1852 by Silas Sheather who leased land adjoining the [[Parramatta River]] on what was originally part of [[Elizabeth Farm]].<ref name="Parramatta Heritage Centre"/> ''Fuller's Sydney Handbook'' of 1877 describes his nursery as having 59 varieties of camellias.<ref name="FloraSEA"/> Camellia and other flowers from Sheather's nursery were sent by [[steamship]] downriver to florists at Sydney Markets, tied in bunches and suspended from long pieces of wood which were hung up about the decks.<ref name="Parramatta Heritage Centre"/><ref name="SMH"/> Silas Sheather developed a number of camellia cultivars, the most popular (and still commercially grown) were [[Camellia japonica 'Prince Frederick William'|''C. japonica'' 'Prince Frederick William']] and ''C. japonica'' 'Harriet Beecher Sheather', named after his daughter.<ref name="FloraSEA"/><ref name="GranvilleGuardian"/> The area in the vicinity of Sheather's nursery was eventually made a suburb and named [[Camellia, New South Wales|Camellia]], in honor of Camellia Grove nursery.<ref name="SydneySuburb"/><ref name="McClymont"/>

By 1883, Shepherd and Company, the leading nurserymen in Australia at the time, listed 160 varieties of ''Camellia japonica''.<ref name="CamelliasInAustralia"/>

Associate Professor [[Eben Gowrie Waterhouse]] was a scholar, linguist, garden designer and camellia expert who brought about a worldwide revival of interest in the genus in the first half of the twentieth century.<ref name="O'Neil">{{cite book|last1=O'Neil|first1=W.M.|title=Eben Gowrie Waterhouse|chapter=Waterhouse, Eben Gowrie (1881–1977)|url=https://adb.anu.edu.au/biography/waterhouse-eben-gowrie-8991|via=Australian Dictionary of Biography|publisher=Australian National University|access-date=19 September 2016|archive-date=19 September 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160919072643/http://adb.anu.edu.au/biography/waterhouse-eben-gowrie-8991|url-status=live}}</ref> The E.G. Waterhouse National Camellia Garden in [[Sydney]], Australia is named after him.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.sutherlandshire.nsw.gov.au/Outdoors/Parks-and-Playgrounds/Parks/E.G.-Waterhouse-National-Camellia-Gardens-Caringbah-South|title=E.G. Waterhouse National Camellia Gardens, Caringbah South - Sutherland Shire Council|website=www.sutherlandshire.nsw.gov.au|archive-date=23 September 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200923073047/http://www.sutherlandshire.nsw.gov.au/Outdoors/Parks-and-Playgrounds/Parks/E.G.-Waterhouse-National-Camellia-Gardens-Caringbah-South}}</ref>

===Europe===
According to a research conducted in 1959, by Dr. Frederick Meyer, of the United States Department of Agriculture, the camellias of Campo Bello (Portugal) are the oldest known specimens in Europe, which would have been planted around 1550, that is to say, these trees are nowadays approximately 460 years old.<ref>Jorge Garrido: "Portuguese Camellias, History&Beauty" Agro-Manual Publicaçoes, Lda, February 2014. Page: 1</ref> However it is said that the camellia was first brought to the West in 1692 by [[Engelbert Kaempfer]], Chief Surgeon to the Dutch East India Company. He brought details of over 30 varieties back from Asia.{{citation needed|date=August 2021}} Camellias were introduced into Europe during the 18th century and had already been cultivated in the Orient for thousands of years. Robert James of Essex, England, is thought to have brought back the first live camellia to England in 1739. On his return from [[Dejima]], [[Carl Peter Thunberg]] made a short trip to London where he made the acquaintance of [[Sir Joseph Banks]]. Thunberg donated to [[Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew|Kew Botanic Gardens]] four specimens of ''Camellia japonica''. One of these was supposedly given in 1780 to the botanical garden of [[Pillnitz Castle]] near [[Dresden]] in Germany where it currently measures {{convert|8.9|m|ft|abbr=off}} in height and {{convert|11|m|ft|abbr=off}} in diameter.<ref name=camellia/>

[[File:Pillnitz Castle. Camellia japonica 001.jpg|thumb|''Camellia japonica'' in the garden of [[Pillnitz Castle]], Germany]]

The oldest trees of ''Camellia japonica'' in Europe can be found in [[Vila Nova de Gaia|Campobello]] (Portugal), [[Caserta]] (Italy) and [[Pillnitz Castle|Pillnitz]] (Germany).<ref>P. Vela, J. L. Couselo, C. Salinero, M. González, M. J. Sainz: "Morpho-botanic and molecular characterization of the oldest camellia trees in Europe". In: ''International Camellia Journal'', No. 41, 2009, pp. 51-57</ref> These were probably planted at the end of the 16th century.

===United States===

In the U.S., camellias were first sold in 1807 as greenhouse plants, but were soon distributed to be grown outdoors in the south.<ref name="Cothran">Cothran, James R. ''Gardens and historic plants of the antebellum South''. South Carolina: University of South Carolina Press. 2003. pages 166-167. {{ISBN|1-57003-501-6}}</ref>

In Charleston, South Carolina, the estate garden of Magnolia-on-the-Ashley introduced hundreds of new ''Camellia japonica'' cultivars from the 19th century onwards, and its recently restored collection has been designated an International Camellia Garden of Excellence. "Debutante", a popular variety, was originally introduced by Magnolia as "Sarah C. Hastie". The name was changed to give it more marketing appeal.{{citation needed|date=March 2023}}

Cross-breeding of camellias has produced many cultivars which are tolerant of [[hardiness zone]] 6 winters. These camellia varieties can grow in the milder parts of the lower Midwest (St. Louis, for example), Pacific Northwest, NYC area (NYC/NJ/CT), and even Ontario, Canada (near edge of the Great Lakes).{{citation needed|date=March 2023}}

It is the official state flower of the US state of [[Alabama]].<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.meettheusa.com/usa-facts/alabama-facts |title=51 Alabama Facts |publisher=Meet The USA |date=2022 |access-date=2022-07-03 |archive-date=2022-07-03 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220703041510/https://www.meettheusa.com/usa-facts/alabama-facts |url-status=live }}</ref>

==Cultivars==
''Camellia japonica'' is valued for its flowers, which can be single, semi-double or [[double flowered]].<ref name="Cothran" /> There are more than 2,000 [[cultivar]]s developed from ''C. japonica''. The shade of the flowers can vary from red to pink to white; they sometimes have multi-coloured stripes or specks. Cultivars include 'Elegans' with large pink flowers which often have white streaks, 'Giulio Nuccio' with red to pinkish petals and yellow stamens, 'Mathotiana Alba' with pure white flowers, and the light crimson semi-double-flowered [[Camellia japonica 'The Czar'|'The Czar']].<ref name="Vermeulen 65">Nico Vermeulen. ''The Complete Encyclopedia of Container Plants'', pp. 65-66. Rebo International, Netherlands, 1998. {{ISBN|90-366-1584-4}}</ref>

''C. japonica'' 'Alba Plena' is nicknamed the "Bourbon Camellia". Captain Connor of the [[East Indiaman]] {{ship||Carnatic|1787 EIC ship|2}},<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://internationalcamellia.org/camellia-japonica-alba-plena|title=Camellia japonica Alba Plena|website=internationalcamellia.org|access-date=2021-07-12|archive-date=2021-07-12|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210712170130/https://internationalcamellia.org/camellia-japonica-alba-plena|url-status=live}}</ref> brought the flower to England in 1792.<ref>Booth, William B. History and Description of the Species of Camellia and Thea. Published by s.n., 1829. Original from Harvard University. Digitized Jun 4, 2007.</ref> The flowers are pure white and about 3 to 4 inches across. It blooms earlier than most cultivated camellias, in the early winter or spring, and can flower for 4 to 5 months.<ref>The Magazine of horticulture, botany, and all useful discoveries and improvements in rural affairs. Published by Hovey., 1836. v. 2. Original from Harvard University. Digitized May 11, 2007.</ref>

The zig-zag camellia or ''C. japonica'' 'Unryu' has different zig-zag branching patterns. "Unryu" means "dragon in the clouds" in Japanese; the Japanese believe it looks like a dragon climbing up to the sky. Another type of rare camellia is called the fishtail camellia or ''C. japonica'' 'Kingyo-tsubaki'. The tips of the leaves of this plant resemble a fish's tail.<ref>Kirton, Meredith. ''Dig: Modern Australian Gardening''. Murdoch Books, 2004. 399. {{ISBN|1-74045-365-4}}</ref>

===Flower form or style===
Camellia flower forms are quite varied but the main types are single, semi-double, formal double, informal double and elegans (or anemone) form.{{citation needed|date=February 2020}}

====Single====

Single flowers have five to a maximum of eight petals in one row, petals loose, regular or irregular. May include petaloids; prominent display of stamens & pistils.{{citation needed|date=February 2020}}

====Semi-double====
Two or more rows of large regular, irregular or loose outer petals (nine or more) with an uninterrupted cluster of stamens. May include petaloids; petals may overlap or be set in rows for 'hose in hose' effect.{{citation needed|date=February 2020}}

====Formal double====
Many rows and number of petals (sometimes more than a hundred), regularly disposed, tiered or imbricated, but no visible stamens. Usually with a central cone of tightly furled petals.{{citation needed|date=February 2020}}

====Elegans orm====
One or more rows of large outer petals lying flat or undulating, with a mass of intermingled petaloids and stamens in the center. Also called "Anemone Form".{{Citation needed|reason=Can't find any evidence Elegans form is used outside Australia.|date=February 2020}}

A mass of raised petals with petaloids (parts of the flower that have assumed the appearance of small, narrow or twisted petals). Stamens may or may not be visible. Also called "Peony Form".{{citation needed|date=February 2020}}

==Cultivation==
Camellias should be planted in the shade in organic, somewhat acidic, semi-moist but well drained soil. If the soil is not well drained, it can cause the roots to rot.<ref>Francko, David. A. ''Palms won't grow here and other myths''. Oregon: Timber Press, Inc. 2003. {{ISBN|0-88192-575-6}}</ref>

As a ''Camellia'' species, ''C. japonica'' can be used to make tea. Its processed leaves show aromatic fragrance. It contains caffeine and catechins of the same kind as ''C. sinensis''.<ref>Major Components of Teas Manufactured with Leaf and Flower of Korean Native Camellia japonica L. Cha Young-Ju, Lee Jang-Won, Kim Ju-Hee, Park Min-Hee and Lee Sook-Young, Korean Journal of Medicinal Crop Science, Volume 12, Issue 3, 2004, pages 183-190 ([http://www.koreascience.or.kr/article/ArticleFullRecord.jsp?cn=OOJJBO_2004_v12n3_183 abstract in English] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160414133519/http://www.koreascience.or.kr/article/ArticleFullRecord.jsp?cn=OOJJBO_2004_v12n3_183 |date=2016-04-14 }})</ref>

===Diseases===
Some fungal and algal diseases include: Spot Disease, which gives the upper side of leaves a silver color and round spots, and can cause loss of leaves; Black Mold; Leaf Spot; Leaf Gall; Flower Blight, which causes flowers to become brown and fall; Root Rot; and Canker caused by the fungus ''[[Glomerella cingulata]]'', which penetrates plants through wounds. Some insects and pests of ''C. japonica'' are the Fuller Rose Beetle ''Pantomorus cervinus'', the [[mealybugs]] ''Planococcus citri''<ref>{{Cite web |title=Sanitary status of camellias growing at the urban parks and gardens from the Pazos in Galicia (NW Spain) |url=https://internationalcamellia.org/en-us/caring-for-camellias/sanitary-status-of-camellias-growing |access-date=2025-03-14 |website=internationalcamellia.org |language=en-us}}</ref> and ''Pseudococcus longispinus'', the [[weevils]] ''Otiorhyncus salcatus'' and ''Otiorhyncus ovatus'', and the tea scale ''Fiorinia theae''.{{citation needed|date=March 2023}}

Some physiological diseases include salt injury which results from high levels of salt in soil; [[chlorosis]] which is thought to be caused lack of certain elements in the soil or insufficient acidity preventing their absorption by the roots; bud drop which causes loss or decay of buds, and can be caused by over-watering, high temperatures, or pot-bound roots. Other diseases are [[oedema]] and sunburn. Not much is known about viral diseases in ''C. japonica''.<ref>Pirone, Pascal P. Diseases and pests of ornamental plants. Edition 5. John Wiley and Sons. 1978. 172-175.</ref>

''C. japonica'' leaves are eaten by the [[caterpillar]]s of some [[Lepidoptera]], such as the [[Engrailed (moth)|engrailed]] (''Ectropis crepuscularia'').{{citation needed|date=March 2023}}

== Use by humans ==
Camellias are used to make teas and medicinal tinctures. See the overview at [[Camellia#History and use|Uses of Camellia]].

==In culture and art==
[[File:Japan 1961 Camellia.jpg|thumb|''C. japonica'' on a Japanese postage stamp.]]
[[File:0-Camellia japonica Mt.NIshigatake .Tambasasayama,西ヶ嶽落ち椿 22724.jpg|thumb|Ochi Tsubaki]]
In [[Japanese literature]], camellia flowers unfurling in early spring symbolise the virtue of resilience and beauty in modesty, while the whole flowers dropping off the camellia plants (''ochi tsubaki''<ref>{{Cite web |date=2021-12-17 |title=Another language to look through |url=https://www.odt.co.nz/lifestyle/home-garden/another-language-look-through |access-date=2026-01-13 |website=Otago Daily Times Online News |language=en}}</ref>) are likened to a beheaded [[samurai]]'s head.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Japan |first=Deeply Regional |date=2020-08-01 |title=Of beauty and blood: Camellia, the other floral icon of Japan |url=https://www.deeplyregionaljapan.com/single-post/of-beauty-and-blood-camellia-the-other-floral-icon-of-japan |access-date=2025-03-14 |website=tour-operator |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=LaSpina |first=David |date=2017-11-23 |title=Falling Camellia :: Haiku of Japan #41 |url=https://steemit.com/poetry/@dbooster/falling-camilla-haiku-of-japan-41 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250318122009/https://steemit.com/poetry/@dbooster/falling-camilla-haiku-of-japan-41 |archive-date=18 March 2025 |access-date=2025-03-14 |website=Steemit |language=en}}</ref> The [[Furutsubaki-no-rei]] is a japanese [[yōkai]] said to develop from old camellia trees.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Furutsubaki no rei {{!}} Yokai.com |url=https://yokai.com/furutsubakinorei/ |access-date=2025-03-14 |website=yokai.com}}</ref>

Camellias are seen as lucky symbols for the [[Chinese New Year]] and spring and were even used as offerings to the gods during the Chinese New Year. It is also thought that Chinese women would never wear a Camellia in their hair because it opened much later after the bud formed. This was thought to signify that she would not have a son for a long time.<ref name="Valder" />

The following is a poem written by English evangelical Protestant writer [[Charlotte Elizabeth Tonna]] in 1834:<ref name="Elizabeth" />

<blockquote><poem>
THE WHITE CAMELLIA JAPONICA.
Thou beauteous child of purity and grace,
  What element could yield so fair a birth?
Defilement bore me — my abiding place
  Was mid the foul clods of polluted earth.
But light looked on me from a holier sphere,
  To draw me heavenward — then I rose and shone;
And can I vainly to thine eye appear,
  Thou dust-born gazer? make the type thine own.
From thy dark dwelling look thou forth, and see
  The purer beams that brings a lovelier change for thee.
</poem></blockquote>
